status: proposed teaching and verification plan; not a delivered lesson
title: Impulse and center-of-mass motion
objective: Integrate force to obtain impulse and use a system's external impulse to predict total momentum and center-of-mass motion.
alignment: Develops the official PHS 231 momentum topic in the researched course scope. Teaching sequence, examples, investigation, generators, and assessment defaults are proposed for this platform and are not an official NU syllabus or grading policy.

prerequisites.purpose: Time derivatives, signed areas, and definite integration
Inertial observers and Galilean velocity changes
Recipient-specific force inventories and Newton's third law
Distinguish work from impulse and kinetic energy from momentum
System boundaries and internal energy conversion
Develop the exact integral operations required here while linking to calculus preparation when available

coverage.teaching: Define p=mv for positive constant mass in a chosen inertial frame. Preserve signed components in one, two, and three dimensions. Compare momentum and kinetic energy: equal speed reversals change momentum, while equal momenta at different masses need not imply equal kinetic energy.
critical: Use kg m/s, equivalent to N s, not joules.
A vector sum is not the sum of speed magnitudes.

coverage.teaching: Integrate dp/dt=Fnet over a time interval to get Jnet=pf-pi. Separate impulse by a named force from net impulse. Derive final velocity, distinguish average and peak forces, and state constant-mass conditions.
critical: Force-time area is impulse; force-position area is work.
Impulse direction follows vector change, not necessarily the final velocity.
For a vehicle losing mass, track a closed collection or account for momentum flux; do not apply a fixed-mass vehicle formula blindly.

coverage.teaching: Evaluate constant, triangular, piecewise signed, and polynomial force histories. Show that equal impulses can have different peak forces and transient motion. Compare duration changes at fixed impulse and fixed shape with changes of shape at fixed duration.
critical: Net zero impulse can contain large opposing contributions.
A longer duration fixes a smaller average force at fixed impulse, but does not by itself determine the peak without a shape condition.
Neglect of external impulses during a brief interaction needs a scale comparison.

coverage.teaching: Specify a constant-mass system and add its particle equations. Internal pairs cancel in total momentum under the Newtonian third-law assumptions; external impulse changes total P. A zero external force at every instant gives constant P throughout, while a zero integrated external impulse only matches endpoint totals.
critical: Internal forces can change individual momenta.
Conserved total momentum does not conserve kinetic energy.
A system choice can move an interaction between internal and external categories.

coverage.teaching: Define Rcm=Σmi ri/M, Vcm=P/M, and M Acm=ΣFext for fixed masses and an inertial frame. Work signed coordinates componentwise and use translation and mass-scale invariance. CM need not lie on material, but positive masses place it within their convex hull.
critical: Use mass weights, not an unweighted coordinate average unless masses match.
CM is a geometric/dynamical summary, not necessarily a material particle.
Only external forces govern acceleration of the system CM.

coverage.teaching: Replace sums by M=∫dm and Rcm=(1/M)∫r dm, with line, area, or volume density as appropriate. Derive a linearly varying rod density and use symmetry. Model a hole by subtracting a removed mass distribution, not by claiming negative physical mass.
critical: Require nonnegative density, positive total mass, and correct density units.
Integrate total mass as well as the first moment for nonuniform density.
A removed piece must lie within the original object and leave positive mass.

coverage.teaching: For a frame translating at constant velocity u, show P'=P-Mu and Vcm'=Vcm-u. Derive Ktotal=M|Vcm|²/2+Σmi|vi-Vcm|²/2 by canceling the weighted relative-velocity sum. The internal relative kinetic term is unchanged by a Galilean boost.
critical: The CM frame has zero total momentum, not zero individual velocities or kinetic energy.
External impulse determines CM velocity but not internal energy conversion.
Force resultant times CM displacement accounts for CM kinetic change, not necessarily all work on an extended deforming system.

guided: Use the vertical-contact fixture. Require net impulse, gravity impulse, contact impulse, mean contact force, and recognition that a peak force is not determined without a time profile. Explain why omitting the weight impulse would give the wrong contact average.

investigation.model: A closed constant-mass Newtonian system under a prescribed net external vector pulse. Track CM velocity, momentum, and displacement; do not invent individual trajectories or internal kinetic energy. A single particle is a special case.
investigation.normalizedForce: F(t)=J f(u)/T, u=t/T in[0,1]. Force is zero outside the pulse. Endpoint jumps for constant/front-loaded pulses are finite force jumps, not delta impulses.
accessibleOutput: Signed force-time component plot with labeled axes and selectable displayed component
Equivalent table for force, accumulated impulse, CM velocity, and CM displacement
Peak and mean force comparison across profiles at the same impulse and duration
Keyboard inputs and presets; no motion animation required
domainNotes: For this nonnegative normalized-shape family, J=0 switches the entire pulse off. A general zero-integral force can still have nonzero opposing segments; the lesson and practice cover that case.
Equal impulses fix final momentum at fixed initial state but do not fix displacement, peak force, or the time history.
The system's internal kinetic energy is unspecified. Any CM kinetic quantity must be labeled translational CM energy, not total system energy.
At t=T report the pulse's left-limit force if showing the final shape sample, and separately state that the force is zero after the interval.
investigation.evidence: Keep J fixed and vary T, then compare all four profiles at one duration. Record final CM velocity, peak force, and displacement; explain which results are fixed by impulse and which depend on timing. Include the zero-J model limitation and a worked three-particle CM check in notes.

independentChecks: Geometric signed force-time areas and exact polynomial quadrature
Numerical force and velocity integration for all pulse profiles, including piecewise joins and endpoints
Momentum sums before and after inertial-frame changes
Translation, uniform mass scaling, and convex-hull bounds for CM
Independent positive-region decomposition of plate cutouts
Continuous mass and first-moment quadrature with λ≥0
Internal impulse cancellation and kinetic-energy decomposition
Independent gravity correction for contact versus net impulse
Equivalent exact expressions, radicals, invalid values, units, and complete component responses
edges: nonzero pulses with zero net impulse
zero vector in the normalized pulse model
pulse joins and one-sided endpoint force values
α=-1 density with one zero endpoint
physically valid cutout boundaries and positive remaining mass
relative velocities and nonzero CM-frame kinetic energy
